completes.meta_description: Shop complete fingerboards ready to ride: wooden decks, tuned trucks, bearing wheels. Every fingerboard setup quality-checked before it ships.
completes.intro: A fingerboard complete is the fastest way to get rolling — deck, trucks, wheels and grip already assembled and tuned. Every complete here is hand-picked for a specific riding style, from the best fingerboard for beginners to a professional fingerboard complete built for serious sessions.

buying_guide.heading: Width: the spec that matters most
buying_guide.body: Deck width sets the feel of the whole fingerboard setup. A 34mm complete fingerboard is the most versatile choice, suiting street tricks, park lines and everything in between. Drop to 32mm for tight technical riding; go wider at 36mm for a planted, stable feel on bigger obstacles. Trucks are matched to deck width here, so you never end up with a mismatched setup that wobbles on grinds.

buying_guide.heading: Concave and kicks
buying_guide.body: Concave is the curve across the deck your fingers sit in. Deeper concave gives more lock-in and flick for flip tricks. A shallower concave with a steep kick produces faster pop for street-style lines. Every complete fingerboard listing describes the concave profile so you can match the geometry to how you actually ride.

buying_guide.heading: Why bearing wheels matter
buying_guide.body: Real bearing wheels are the single most important upgrade on any cheap fingerboard. Hollow plastic hubs spin briefly and feel dead. Bearing wheels roll freely and respond to finger pressure. Every complete fingerboard in this collection ships with bearing wheels as standard — that alone separates these setups from budget toy-store options.

buying_guide.heading: Wood vs. plastic construction
buying_guide.body: A wooden fingerboard complete built from maple plies behaves like a scaled skateboard in a way moulded plastic cannot. The wood flexes, pops and responds to finger pressure in a way that builds real muscle memory. The difference in feel is immediate from the first ollie.

faqs.q: What size complete fingerboard should I start with?
faqs.a: 34mm is the right starting point for most riders — the most common all-round size and the easiest to find matching parts for. Once you know how you ride, move to 32mm for tighter street lines or 36mm for a wider park feel.

faqs.q: Are complete fingerboards good for beginners?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the complete uses real components rather than moulded plastic. A wooden fingerboard complete with bearing wheels gives accurate feedback and builds technique that transfers when you move to custom setups.

faqs.q: Can I upgrade parts on a complete fingerboard?
faqs.a: Every part on a quality complete is swappable. Trucks, wheels, bearings and bushings come off with a standard fingerboard tool. Most riders swap bushings first — the cheapest way to change how a board rides without buying a new setup.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a fingerboard setup and a complete?
faqs.a: They mean the same thing. A complete is a deck assembled with trucks and wheels, ready to ride. Some riders use 'setup' to describe a custom build they assembled themselves, but the terms are interchangeable in most shops.

faqs.q: Do cheap fingerboards come with bearings?
faqs.a: Most budget fingerboards use hollow plastic hubs, which is why they feel flat and unresponsive. The completes here all use genuine bearing wheels — check the product description if a listing does not specify.

decks.meta_description: Maple fingerboard decks in every width. 32mm, 34mm and 36mm pro fingerboard decks, blank and graphic. Hand-picked wooden fingerboard decks for real riding.
decks.intro: The fingerboard deck is the foundation every build starts from. This collection covers blank fingerboard decks for riders who want a canvas, graphic pro fingerboard decks for those who care about aesthetics, and wooden fingerboard decks in every width from 32mm to 36mm.

buying_guide.heading: Choosing your deck width
buying_guide.body: A 32mm fingerboard deck suits tight, fast street riding where you want the board to whip quickly. The 34mm fingerboard deck is the standard all-round width — the majority of pros ride somewhere in this range, and it is the easiest size to find matching trucks for. A 36mm fingerboard deck gives a wider, more planted feel that works well for park lines and larger obstacles.

buying_guide.heading: Concave profiles explained
buying_guide.body: Concave is the curve across the width of the deck. Deeper concave locks your fingers in for flip tricks and gives more control during technical lines. A shallower concave with a steeper kick produces faster pop — useful for street-style riding where you want the nose and tail to snap quickly. Each deck listing here describes the concave so you can match it to your technique.

buying_guide.heading: Blank vs. graphic decks
buying_guide.body: A blank fingerboard deck is unprinted maple — clean, simple and often slightly cheaper than a graphic option. Blank decks suit riders who want to apply custom grip patterns or paint the board themselves. Graphic pro fingerboard decks use the same maple construction as blanks; the difference is purely cosmetic, not structural.

buying_guide.heading: Why wood matters
buying_guide.body: A wooden fingerboard deck built from cross-laminated maple veneer presses into shape under heat and pressure. The layered construction gives a realistic flex and pop that plastic cannot replicate. When you pop an ollie on a properly made maple deck, the tail springs back in a way that builds genuine technique.

faqs.q: What width fingerboard deck should I buy?
faqs.a: 34mm is the safest starting point — it matches the widest range of trucks and suits most riding styles. Go to 32mm for a narrower, faster setup for technical tricks, or 36mm for a wider, more stable platform for park lines.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a 32mm and 34mm fingerboard deck?
faqs.a: 2mm sounds small but is noticeable underfoot. A 32mm deck feels snappier for technical flip tricks; 34mm sits wider and gives more surface area for your fingers. Most riders find 34mm easier to learn on and stay there.

faqs.q: Do I need special trucks for different deck widths?
faqs.a: Yes. A 34mm fingerboard deck pairs with 34mm trucks, a 32mm deck with 32mm trucks. Trucks that are too narrow feel unstable on grinds; trucks that are too wide catch your fingers unexpectedly. Width matching is one of the most basic rules of fingerboard setup.

faqs.q: Are blank fingerboard decks the same quality as graphic ones?
faqs.a: Generally yes — the construction is identical and the blank just skips the printing step. Some blanks are offcuts from a graphic run, which can make them slightly cheaper. Wood, concave and kicks are the same.

faqs.q: How many plies should a fingerboard deck have?
faqs.a: Most quality wooden fingerboard decks use five to seven maple plies. More plies in a thinner press gives a stiffer deck with sharper pop; fewer plies give more flex. The ply count is usually listed in the product specs.

trucks.meta_description: Pro fingerboard trucks in 32mm, 34mm and more. Inverted kingpin and classic designs, quality-checked. The best fingerboard trucks matched to your deck width.
trucks.intro: Fingerboard trucks are where a build either comes together or falls apart. The wrong width wobbles on grinds, soft bushings wander, and cheap metal bends under pressure. Every pair here is hand-picked for precise geometry, consistent axle spacing and hardware that holds up to real sessions.

buying_guide.heading: Match your truck width to your deck
buying_guide.body: The most important rule with fingerboard trucks is width matching. A pair of 34mm fingerboard trucks belongs on a 34mm deck; 32mm fingerboard trucks go on a 32mm deck. Trucks narrower than your deck feel twitchy during grinds; trucks that overhang the deck edge catch your fingers at the wrong moment. Always check the deck width before adding trucks to your cart.

buying_guide.heading: Inverted kingpin vs. regular kingpin
buying_guide.body: On regular kingpin trucks, the bolt head sits outside the hanger where it can snag on ledges and rails. Inverted kingpin (IKP) fingerboard trucks tuck the bolt inside the hanger, removing that catch point entirely. For riders who focus on grinds and slides, IKP trucks make lines cleaner and reduce the bails caused by hardware catching an obstacle.

buying_guide.heading: Single axle trucks
buying_guide.body: Single axle fingerboard trucks use a one-piece axle rod rather than the two-part construction found on standard trucks. This removes a potential failure point and gives a cleaner grind surface. Both designs perform well at the pro level — the choice is largely personal preference and aesthetic.

buying_guide.heading: Bushings and how they affect turn
buying_guide.body: The bushings inside your trucks control how the board turns. Lower durometer — 70A — is softer and makes trucks carve freely. Higher durometer at 75A or above stiffens them for faster lines and bigger obstacles. Swapping bushings is cheaper than buying new pro fingerboard trucks and is the first adjustment most riders make when a setup feels wrong.

faqs.q: What are the best fingerboard trucks for beginners?
faqs.a: Standard kingpin trucks in 34mm are the most beginner-friendly — the widest-produced size, easy to find replacement parts for, and predictable in turn geometry. Once you are comfortable, try IKP designs or different bushing hardnesses to dial in the feel.

faqs.q: Do fingerboard trucks and wheels have to match?
faqs.a: The axle diameter determines which wheels fit. Most pro fingerboard trucks and wheels use a standard axle size, so mixing brands is usually straightforward. When buying fingerboard trucks and wheels separately, check that the wheel bore diameter matches the axle.

faqs.q: How do I know if my fingerboard trucks are too loose or too tight?
faqs.a: Lean the board on a flat surface and push lightly from one side. Sharp carve from a small push means loose trucks; barely turning means tight. Adjust the kingpin nut first; swap bushings if nut adjustment alone does not give the feel you want.

faqs.q: Can I use 34mm trucks on a 32mm deck?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but the trucks will overhang the deck edges, creating an uneven grind surface and making flip tricks feel off. Width matching is the standard recommendation — stick to 32mm fingerboard trucks on a 32mm deck.

wheels.meta_description: Urethane fingerboard wheels with real bearings. CNC and cast options, pro fingerboard wheels in multiple shapes and hardnesses. Ready to roll.
wheels.intro: Fingerboard wheels are the part most riders underestimate until they try a proper set. Urethane fingerboard wheels with real bearings spin longer, respond to finger pressure, and give the board a liveliness that hollow plastic hubs cannot produce.

buying_guide.heading: Bearings: the spec that changes everything
buying_guide.body: Fingerboard bearing wheels contain a miniature ABEC-rated bearing inside each hub. The bearing allows the wheel to spin freely with almost no resistance, giving the board momentum during tricks and making landings feel alive. Fingerboard wheels with bearings are the single most noticeable upgrade you can make to a budget setup. All wheels in this collection use genuine bearings, not hollow hubs.

buying_guide.heading: Urethane vs. plastic construction
buying_guide.body: Urethane fingerboard wheels grip the surface slightly, absorb small imperfections in obstacles, and compress just enough on landing to feel realistic. CNC fingerboard wheels are machined for precise tolerances, meaning all four wheels in a set are genuinely identical in diameter — consistent roll and landing feel. Plastic wheels slide unpredictably and produce a flat, toy-like response.

buying_guide.heading: Wheel shape and size
buying_guide.body: A smaller, harder wheel rolls quickly on smooth surfaces and suits technical street riding. A larger, slightly softer wheel handles rougher surfaces and gives a smoother ride across obstacles. The best fingerboard wheels for your style depend on what surfaces you skate and which tricks you focus on. Check diameter and durometer in each listing.

buying_guide.heading: Replacing bearings
buying_guide.body: Fingerboard bearings are the most common wear item on any setup. They can be pressed out, cleaned with a small amount of bearing lubricant, and pressed back in — or replaced entirely when they feel gritty or slow. Keeping spare bearings on hand means worn wheels do not retire your whole setup.

faqs.q: What are the best fingerboard wheels for street skating?
faqs.a: Smaller, harder urethane wheels suit technical street tricks where speed and spin matter more than grip. A higher durometer rating means the wheel slides more predictably on ledges and rails. Pro fingerboard wheels in the 57–60 durometer range are a common street choice.

faqs.q: Do fingerboard wheels come with bearings already installed?
faqs.a: Most pro fingerboard wheels are sold with bearings pre-installed and ready to mount. Some are sold wheel-only with bearings available separately. Wheels at Fingerboard Lab specify whether bearings are included in the listing.

faqs.q: How do I know if my fingerboard wheels need new bearings?
faqs.a: Spin a wheel by hand and listen. A healthy bearing spins smoothly with a quiet hiss. A dry bearing produces a rough, grinding sound and slows within a second or two. Gritty bearings can often be saved by cleaning and adding a small drop of thin bearing oil.

faqs.q: Are CNC fingerboard wheels worth the extra cost?
faqs.a: CNC wheels are cut to precise dimensions, so all four in a set are genuinely identical in diameter. Even a small difference between front and back wheel diameter changes how the board rolls and lands. If consistency matters to your riding, CNC wheels are worth it.

faqs.q: Can I use fingerboard wheels from different brands?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the bore diameter matches your axle size. Most pro fingerboard wheels and trucks follow the same standard axle dimension, so mixing brands is common. Check the bore size in the product description against your truck axle diameter when in doubt.

grip-tape.meta_description: Foam grip tape for fingerboards in uncut sheets and pre-cut sizes. Best fingerboard grip tape for feel and flip control. Riptape-style and textured options.
grip-tape.intro: Fingerboard grip tape is foam, not sandpaper — a fact that surprises most people new to the hobby. The foam surface grips your fingertips without tearing your skin, and the texture directly affects how flip tricks feel and how cleanly your fingers release from the board.

buying_guide.heading: How foam grip tape works
buying_guide.body: Foam grip tape for fingerboards uses a thin textured foam layer with a pressure-sensitive adhesive backing. The foam compresses slightly under finger contact, giving grip without abrasion. Finer foam grip tape gives a faster release, which suits flip-trick-heavy riding; coarser textures give more grip for grinds and slides where control matters more than quick flick.

buying_guide.heading: Uncut sheets vs. pre-cut strips
buying_guide.body: Uncut sheets of fingerboard tape let you trim to your exact deck shape — useful for unusual widths or if you want a specific grip area. Pre-cut strips are quicker to apply and sized for standard deck widths. If you build your own decks or run unusual shapes, an uncut sheet is the right choice. For standard decks, pre-cut options waste less material.

buying_guide.heading: Applying grip tape cleanly
buying_guide.body: Start from one end and lay the grip down in one smooth motion, pressing from the centre outward to avoid air bubbles. Trim overhang with a sharp blade run flat against the deck edge. Most foam fingerboard grip tape allows repositioning within the first few seconds before the adhesive sets fully.

buying_guide.heading: When to replace your grip
buying_guide.body: Grip wears from the nose and tail outward. When the texture flattens to the point where tricks feel inconsistent — especially kick flips where release timing matters — it is time to replace. Peel from the tail at a low angle to lift the adhesive cleanly without leaving residue.

faqs.q: What is the best fingerboard grip tape?
faqs.a: It depends on riding style. Riders focused on technical flip tricks prefer finer foam for quicker release; those who focus on grinds lean toward coarser foam for more control. A mid-texture foam works well across both styles — try one sheet before committing to a bulk order.

faqs.q: Is fingerboard grip tape the same as riptape?
faqs.a: Riptape is a brand name that became shorthand for foam fingerboard grip tape. Riptape fingerboard products use foam construction, and most riders use the words interchangeably. Other brands make functionally similar foam grip tape — check the texture description to compare.

faqs.q: How do I cut foam grip tape to fit my deck?
faqs.a: Place the sheet face-down, lay the deck face-down on top, and trace the outline lightly with a pen. A sharp craft knife gives the cleanest result. Cut slightly inside your line to avoid overhang, then trim any excess after application.

faqs.q: Can I put fingerboard tape on a plastic deck?
faqs.a: Yes. The adhesive on foam fingerboard grip tape bonds to most clean, dry surfaces including plastic. Wipe the deck with a dry cloth first to remove dust and oils. Adhesion on plastic is slightly weaker than on wood, so press the edges down firmly.

tuning-hardware.meta_description: Fingerboard bushings, screws, spacers and tools for tuning your setup. Hand-picked fingerboard parts that make a real difference to how your board rides.
tuning-hardware.intro: The smallest fingerboard parts make a disproportionate difference to how a setup feels. Swapping fingerboard bushings changes the turn character of your trucks in minutes; the right fingerboard tool makes every adjustment precise rather than a guess.

buying_guide.heading: Bushings: durometer explained
buying_guide.body: Fingerboard bushings control how freely your trucks pivot. A lower durometer like 70A is soft and allows the trucks to turn sharply with little pressure. A higher durometer such as 75A or above resists turning and gives a stiffer, more stable ride. Swapping bushings is the cheapest form of fingerboard tuning available — far less than new trucks and immediately transformative. Keep a few hardnesses in your kit to dial in conditions.

buying_guide.heading: Screws, spacers and pivot cups
buying_guide.body: Fingerboard screws attach the baseplate to the deck; worn or stripped screws cause trucks to feel loose regardless of how tight the kingpin is. Fingerboard spacers maintain consistent wheel spacing so bearing wheels spin freely without side-to-side play. Pivot cups wear quietly — when the hanger starts to rattle independently of the baseplate, replacing the pivot cup restores the tight, responsive feel of new trucks at a fraction of the cost.

buying_guide.heading: The right fingerboard tool
buying_guide.body: A proper fingerboard screwdriver or T-tool fits the tiny hardware on pro-spec setups without rounding the heads. Using an undersized flathead is the fastest way to strip a screw that is otherwise fine. A dedicated fingerboard tool costs little and pays for itself the first time it saves a screw. Most tools are double-ended, covering both the kingpin nut and the deck screws.

buying_guide.heading: Fingerboard hardware as a tuning system
buying_guide.body: Experienced riders treat fingerboard hardware as a set of variables rather than a fixed spec. Bushing hardness, kingpin tension, spacer width and screw torque all interact. A setup that feels stiff might just need softer bushings, not new trucks. Working through these adjustments systematically — kingpin first, then bushings, then hardware — is how riders build a setup that feels dialled rather than factory default.

faqs.q: How do I know what hardness fingerboard bushings to use?
faqs.a: If you want loose, carvy trucks for flow riding, go softer — around 70A. For stable trucks on fast lines and big obstacles, go harder at 75A or above. Most riders find the middle range around 73A works across most scenarios. Bushings are inexpensive — buy two or three hardnesses and experiment.

faqs.q: What does a fingerboard tool actually do?
faqs.a: A fingerboard tool has heads sized for the specific hardware used on pro setups — typically a T-wrench for the kingpin nut and a screwdriver for deck mounting screws. The correct fit prevents rounding the hardware. Some designs also include a bearing press end for removing and installing wheel bearings.

faqs.q: How often should I replace fingerboard parts like bushings?
faqs.a: Replace when performance drops. Bushings lose elasticity over time and start to feel dead rather than springy; screws strip when over-tightened. Inspect your hardware every few weeks if you ride often. Small fingerboard hardware is inexpensive enough that replacing early is better than riding a degraded setup.

faqs.q: Where do I start with fingerboard tuning?
faqs.a: Start with the kingpin nut: too loose and the board wanders; too tight and it will not turn. Once the turn feels right, swap bushing hardness to fine-tune. Address hardware and spacers last — only if you notice play or rattling after everything else is adjusted.

ramps-obstacles.meta_description: Fingerboard obstacles for every style: ramps, rails, ledges, quarter pipes, stairs and more. Wooden fingerboard ramps built to pro scale and quality-checked.
ramps-obstacles.intro: A fingerboard ramp or obstacle changes what the board can do — suddenly there are lines to link, not just flat-ground tricks to repeat. This collection covers individual fingerboard obstacles from grind rails to quarter pipes, half pipes, ledges, stairs and manual pads, hand-picked for scale accuracy and surface quality.

buying_guide.heading: Rails and grind obstacles
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard grind rail is one of the most-used obstacles in any setup because grinds are fundamental to the style. Rail height, diameter and surface finish all affect the trick. Fingerboard rail obstacles here specify material and diameter in the listing. Metal rails give the sharpest grind feel; waxed wood surfaces work well for nose grinds and noseslides.

buying_guide.heading: Quarter pipes and half pipes
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard quarter pipe needs a smooth, consistent curve to roll up and land back on cleanly. Poorly constructed ramps have flat spots that interrupt the line. A fingerboard half pipe doubles the setup, allowing lip tricks on both sides across a compact footprint. Wooden fingerboard ramps with a laminate surface outlast painted MDF alternatives — the surface stays smooth through thousands of runs.

buying_guide.heading: Ledges, manual pads and stairs
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard ledge lets you skate waxed marble or concrete textures in miniature. A fingerboard manual pad is flat on top with a slight bevel at entry and exit, built specifically for nose manuals, tail manuals and manual-to-trick combinations. Fingerboard stairs combined with a rail create multi-element lines that mimic real street skating more closely than any single obstacle can.

buying_guide.heading: Building a modular setup
buying_guide.body: Most riders start with a single fingerboard obstacle and add pieces as their skating develops. A grind rail or small ledge is the natural first purchase; quarter pipes become relevant once flat-ground tricks are consistent. The obstacles here are designed at a consistent scale so pieces sit together naturally on a flat surface.

faqs.q: What fingerboard obstacles should I buy first?
faqs.a: A fingerboard grind rail is the most versatile single obstacle — every riding style uses it. A small ledge is the next most-used piece for street riders. If you skate transition rather than street, a quarter pipe replaces the rail as the first purchase.

faqs.q: How big are fingerboard ramps in real dimensions?
faqs.a: Most fingerboard ramps are built to roughly 1:8 scale, compatible with standard 32–36mm decks. A full-size quarter pipe translates to roughly 12–18cm tall for a fingerboard version. Check the height, width and transition radius listed in each product description.

faqs.q: What is a fingerboard quarter pipe used for?
faqs.a: A fingerboard quarter pipe is a curved ramp that transitions from flat ground to vertical, used for rolling up into aerial tricks, stalls and lip tricks at the top. It is the fundamental park obstacle in fingerboarding. A fingerboard half pipe is two quarter pipes facing each other — larger footprint, more trick variety.

faqs.q: Do fingerboard obstacles work on any surface?
faqs.a: Most work best on a smooth, flat surface — a table, desk or a foam or acrylic mat. On rough surfaces, obstacles shift during skating and the board catches on surface irregularities between the obstacle and the ground. A smooth mat beneath the setup keeps everything stable.

faqs.q: Can I mix obstacles from different brands?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the scale is consistent. Most pro-level fingerboard obstacles are built to a compatible scale, so mixing a rail from one maker with a ledge from another is common. Height is the most important spec for visual consistency when pieces sit side by side.

park-kits.meta_description: Complete fingerboard skatepark kits with rails, ramps, ledges and more. Build a full fingerboard park at home. Wooden and modular park sets, quality-checked.
park-kits.intro: A fingerboard skatepark kit gives you everything needed for a full session setup in one box — rails, ramps, ledges, stairs and transition pieces at a consistent scale. Whether you want a compact street plaza or a full fingerboard park with transition, there is a kit here that matches the space you have and the style you skate.

buying_guide.heading: What comes in a fingerboard park kit?
buying_guide.body: Most fingerboard park kits include at least one rail or grind element, a ramp — usually a quarter pipe or small kicker — and a flat obstacle such as a ledge or manual pad. Larger fingerboard park kit options add stairs, half pipes and additional grind surfaces. The description for each kit lists every piece included and gives assembled dimensions, so you know before buying whether the setup fits your desk.

buying_guide.heading: Street plaza vs. transition layouts
buying_guide.body: A street-focused fingerboard skatepark kit emphasises ledges, rails, stairs and manual pads for technical line skating. A transition-focused fingerboard park includes quarter pipes, half pipes and banks for flow skating and aerial tricks. Most kits lean one way or the other. Modular systems let you add transition to a street setup over time, building toward a full fingerboard playground across multiple orders.

buying_guide.heading: Wooden park kits vs. mixed-material sets
buying_guide.body: A wooden fingerboard park is generally more durable than a mixed plastic-and-wood alternative. Wood surfaces can be sanded if they roughen over time, and wooden pieces are heavier and more stable — obstacles do not shift mid-trick. Mixed-material kits are lighter and easier to transport, which matters if you take your setup to sessions elsewhere.

buying_guide.heading: Scaling up over time
buying_guide.body: Most fingerboard park kits are designed as starting points. The pieces use standard scale so individual obstacles — rails, ledges, extra ramps — slot in without looking out of place. Start with a kit that covers your primary skating style, then add single pieces as your line skating develops.

faqs.q: What is included in a fingerboard skatepark kit?
faqs.a: It depends on the kit, but most include between three and eight individual obstacles: typically a rail, a ramp element, a ledge or manual pad, and sometimes stairs or a bank. Every kit listing at Fingerboard Lab includes a full piece list and assembled dimensions.

faqs.q: What size space do I need for a fingerboard park?
faqs.a: A compact fingerboard park kit fits on a standard desk — roughly 60–80cm wide and 40–50cm deep. Larger sets can span 100cm or more. Check the assembled dimensions listed in the product description, not the box shipping dimensions.

faqs.q: Are Tech Deck ramps compatible with pro fingerboard park kits?
faqs.a: Tech Deck obstacles are built to a slightly different scale and designed for plastic toy fingerboards rather than wooden pro setups. Mixing the two is possible, but the scale difference usually looks and feels off. If you want to upgrade from a Tech Deck park, start with one or two pro pieces alongside it and compare scales before committing to a full set.

faqs.q: Can I build a fingerboard park without buying a kit?
faqs.a: Yes — individual obstacles give full control over layout and style, though they typically cost more than a bundled kit. Kits bundle compatible pieces at a better combined price and are the fastest way to build a functional session setup.

faqs.q: What is a fingerboard playground vs. a fingerboard park?
faqs.a: The terms are used interchangeably. Some shops use 'playground' for smaller, more playful setups; 'park' tends to describe larger session environments. The distinction is not standardised — focus on the piece list and dimensions rather than the label.

deck-building.meta_description: Fingerboard molds, presses, veneer, blanks and building kits. Make your own fingerboard from scratch. The most complete deck-building range in the hobby.
deck-building.intro: Making your own fingerboard deck with a fingerboard mold gives you control over every variable — concave depth, kick angle and ply count. This collection carries fingerboard molds, press kits, veneer, blanks and everything else needed to go from flat maple to a shaped deck.

buying_guide.heading: How a fingerboard mold works
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard mold is a shaped form — machined aluminium or dense resin — that presses glued maple veneer plies into the finished deck shape. It defines the concave curve and the kick angles at nose and tail. Stack your veneer plies with glue between each layer, press in the mold until cured, and the deck holds the shape permanently. Different fingerboard molds produce different concave depths and kick heights.

buying_guide.heading: Press vs. clamps
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard press mold is a matched positive-and-negative pair that sandwiches the veneer stack evenly. Pressing with a dedicated press applies uniform pressure across the entire deck simultaneously, producing consistent concave and preventing edges from lifting during cure. Clamping a single-piece fingerboard mold with separate clamps works but requires care to position clamps evenly. Most fingerboard mold kits include either a press mechanism or hardware recommendations.

buying_guide.heading: Veneer, blanks and glue
buying_guide.body: Fingerboard veneer is thin maple sheet — typically 0.6–1mm per ply — sold in sets sized for deck production. Fingerboard blanks are pre-cut veneer sets, ready to glue and press without additional cutting. Using fingerboard blanks speeds up the build and produces consistent deck outlines, useful when pressing multiple decks from a single fingerboard making kit.

buying_guide.heading: Why buy molds here
buying_guide.body: The two best-known brands in the fingerboard market do not sell deck-pressing molds. This collection is one of the only places to find fingerboard molds, matching presses and all associated supplies — veneer, glue, blanks and tools — together. Whether you are working through a fingerboard building kit for the first time or producing a run of DIY fingerboard decks, the range here covers every stage.

faqs.q: How do I make a fingerboard from scratch?
faqs.a: You need a fingerboard mold, maple veneer, wood glue and a way to apply pressure. Stack three to seven veneer plies with glue between each layer, press until cured, then trim, sand the edges and mount trucks and wheels. Full guides are available in the fingerboard building community online.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a fingerboard mold and a press?
faqs.a: A mold is the shaped form that defines the deck concave and kicks. A press is the mechanism that applies pressure during glue cure. Some fingerboard press mold kits combine both — the two halves of the mold also serve as the press.

faqs.q: What veneer should I use for a DIY fingerboard?
faqs.a: Hard maple is standard — the same species used for full-size decks. Look for fingerboard veneer between 0.6mm and 1mm per ply. Fingerboard veneer sold specifically for deck building is pre-cut and graded for grain direction, saving time compared to sourcing raw sheet and cutting it yourself.

faqs.q: Can I press a fingerboard without a dedicated press?
faqs.a: Many builders use a single-piece fingerboard mold with C-clamps. The key is even pressure across the full surface during cure — uneven clamping causes flat spots in the concave. A dedicated fingerboard press mold applies even pressure automatically and is worth buying if you plan to press more than a few decks.

faqs.q: How is making your own fingerboard different from buying one?
faqs.a: With a fingerboard mold kit, you choose the concave depth, kick height, ply count and finish. The process takes roughly an hour of active work plus several hours of cure time. Most builders find skating something they made themselves a fundamentally different experience.

storage-display.meta_description: Fingerboard cases, bags, display stands and storage. Keep your collection protected and on show. Hand-picked for collectors and active riders.
storage-display.intro: A fingerboard case protects a setup worth far more than the case itself — deck graphics fade, trucks scratch and wheels flat-spot when a board rattles loose in a bag or drawer. This collection covers hard and soft fingerboard cases, fingerboard bags for travelling to sessions, and display stands for collectors who want boards visible rather than buried in a box.

buying_guide.heading: Hard cases vs. fingerboard bags
buying_guide.body: A hard fingerboard case offers the best protection during transport — the shell absorbs impacts and keeps the board from shifting internally. Hard cases suit riders who travel to sessions by bike or public transport where the board might get knocked around. A fingerboard bag is lighter, more flexible, and often holds multiple boards alongside a complete. Bags suit riders who skate nearby and want something that sits easily in a backpack.

buying_guide.heading: Storing parts and hardware
buying_guide.body: Loose fingerboard parts — spare bushings, bearings, screws and spacers — disappear faster than almost any other small item. A fingerboard storage case or bag with an internal pocket or divided compartment keeps hardware organised. If you carry a fingerboard tool and spare parts to sessions, look for a case with dedicated hardware storage.

buying_guide.heading: Display stands for collectors
buying_guide.body: A fingerboard display stand holds one or more decks upright and visible, protecting the graphics from contact damage. Acrylic stands are the most common format — transparent, so the deck graphic becomes the visual focus rather than the stand. Wall-mounted display options let boards be arranged like art for larger collections. A proper fingerboard display stand preserves both the condition and the presentation of graphic or limited-release decks.

buying_guide.heading: Travelling with setups
buying_guide.body: The small size of fingerboards means they fit in hand luggage without issue. The main concern in transit is truck and wheel damage from the board moving freely. A case or bag with foam or fabric padding prevents truck scratching and keeps wheels from flat-spotting against a hard surface.

faqs.q: What is the best way to store fingerboards?
faqs.a: A fingerboard case or padded bag protects the deck graphic, prevents truck scratching and keeps the setup dust-free. For long-term storage, keep boards out of direct sunlight — UV fades graphics and can warp thin maple decks over time.

faqs.q: Can I display fingerboards on a wall?
faqs.a: Yes. Wall-mounted fingerboard display stands hold decks horizontally or vertically using minimal hardware. The deck rests in a slot or on small pegs that contact only the trucks or deck edge, keeping the graphic untouched. Check the specs if you have unusually wide or narrow decks.

faqs.q: How many fingerboards fit in a fingerboard bag?
faqs.a: Most single fingerboard bags hold one complete setup. Larger fingerboard storage bags designed for collectors can hold three to six boards. Deck-only storage is more compact than complete setups because trucks add width. Check the listed capacity before buying if you plan to carry more than one board.

faqs.q: Do fingerboard cases come with padding?
faqs.a: Quality fingerboard cases include foam or fabric padding that prevents rattling and protects the deck surface and trucks. Some have pre-cut foam inserts shaped to a specific format; others use flexible padding for different sizes. Check the product description for padding type if scratch protection is a priority.
